cards.front: Why are roads banked at curves?
cards.back: Banking supplies part of the required centripetal force through the horizontal component of the normal force, reducing dependence on friction and preventing outward skidding.

cards.front: Define the angle of banking θ for a road.
cards.back: The angle θ that the road surface makes with the horizontal so that the normal force has a component toward the center of the curve.

cards.front: For a frictionless banked road, which force component equals mg?
State the optimum speed v on a banked curve of radius r and banking angle θ (no friction).
Derive $\tan \theta = v^2/(rg)$ for a frictionless banked road.
cards.back: Resolve forces: $N \cos \theta = mg$ and $N \sin \theta = mv^2/r$. Divide the two equations: $\tan \theta = v^2/(rg)$.

cards.front: On a banked road, in which direction does friction act when speed exceeds the optimum value?
cards.back: Down the slope (opposing the tendency to slide up).

cards.front: Derive the maximum speed on a banked road with coefficient of friction μ.
cards.back: $$v_{\max} = \sqrt{rg \frac{\tan \theta + \mu}{1 - \mu \tan \theta}}$$ obtained by adding friction down the incline to the centripetal equation and solving for v.

cards.front: What occurs if a vehicle travels slower than the optimum speed on a banked road?
cards.back: It tends to slide down the slope; friction then acts up the slope to supply extra centripetal force.
